title: The spacecraft, or the sensors?
task: Say what could make three readings fall in the same second.
scene: Nine minutes after the bang, three cabin pressure readings fall in the same second. Cabin pressure is how hard the air inside is pushing on the walls, and it drops when air leaks out. The dial gauge beside them, which is a needle on a spring rather than anything electrical, has not moved.
question: What could make all three readings fall in the same second?
takeaway: Three readings that fall together are one event. What they share is where to look first.
why: Three holes appearing in the same second is not a thing that happens. One fault behind all three is. So the question becomes what those three have in common, and the answer is the circuit they all run off. There is a check available, and it is the dial gauge.
answerText: One thing all three share — the circuit that powers them. A real leak would move the dial gauge too.

choices: The circuit that all three run off
Three separate holes in the cabin wall
The crew opening a valve somewhere
The dial gauge being read wrongly
rebuttals: Three holes in the same second is not a thing that happens.
A valve would move the dial gauge as well, and it has not moved.
The dial gauge is the one that disagrees, and it is the one working.
text.headline: Mission Control receives a sudden cabin-pressure warning on several digital channels.

title: Build the first picture
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to happen.
scene: Three consoles hold numbers that disagree. One of the two main power lines reads zero. The guidance computer, which keeps track of where the spacecraft is and which way it points, has restarted with no memory of what it saw. Nothing has been written down yet.
takeaway: An answer built to survive being wrong has to be built in a particular order.
why: The recordings from across the failure get wiped within minutes, so they are saved before anything is worked out. Units and clocks come next. A tidy answer built from mixed clocks is confidently wrong. Then the estimates, each with a range rather than one number.

rebuttals: Save the recordings first. It is the only step with a deadline set by a machine rather than by people.
Units and clocks second. This is where one shared fault shows up, instead of being fitted into the answer.
Estimates third, each with a range. A single number cannot be argued with or tested.
Commands last, and only the ones that survive every answer the data still allows.
cards: Save the recordings from before and after the failure.
Check the units, the clocks, and what everything depends on.
Work out where it is and how fast, with a range.
Send only the commands that help either way.

title: The reading that cannot wait
task: Make the call before the next mission clock update.
scene: Four screens are showing four problems at once. Camila Reyes wants to know which one the room should watch while the tracking pass — the few minutes when a dish on Earth can measure the spacecraft — comes round.
question: Which reading tells you soonest whether the crew is in danger?
takeaway: Air runs out in minutes. Warmth and power run out in hours, so the air is watched first.
why: All four readings matter. What separates them is how fast each one runs out. Air is the quick one. A hole in the wall of a spacecraft empties the cabin in minutes, and there is no warning after that. The batteries have hours left in them.
answerText: Cabin pressure. A leak empties the cabin in minutes, and nothing else on the board moves that fast.

choices: Cabin pressure
Battery voltage
Cabin temperature
Radio signal strength
rebuttals: Voltage matters, but the batteries have hours in them. Air does not.
The cabin cools over hours. A leak empties it in minutes.
A lost radio is frightening and not fatal. The crew can still fly.

title: Which measurement gives what
task: Match each thing you need to know to the measurement that gives it.
scene: The onboard computer has restarted and the tracking comes and goes. The room has to rebuild where the spacecraft is from whatever can still be measured, and say what each measurement buys.
takeaway: No single measurement gives a position. Each one gives a piece, and the pieces are different shapes.
why: Each measurement answers a different question and none of them answers all of it. Photographing the spacecraft against known stars gives a direction and no distance. Timing a radio pulse out and back gives a distance and no direction.

choices: Photograph it against stars whose places are already known.
Compare the pitch coming back with the pitch sent out.
Time a radio pulse out to it and back again.
Measure the same thing twice, and subtract.
rebuttals: Direction is an angle, and the star camera is the only instrument here that measures one.
Motion toward us or away shows up in the pitch of what comes back, and nowhere else.
A distance is a speed multiplied by a time, which is what the round trip gives you.
Rates come from repeating. Two positions give a speed, and two speeds give a change.
scenarios: How fast it is coming toward us.

title: Rebuild where it is
task: Put the four steps in order.
scene: The computer restarted and lost its bearings. A distance, two angles and a pitch trace remain, recorded on different clocks. The next tracking pass will test whatever the room reconstructs.
takeaway: A useful answer predicts the next measurement, and says how sure it is.
why: Everything goes onto one map and one clock first, or a tidy answer comes out wrong in a way nobody can see. The distance, the angles and the pitch then get fitted together. Each pins down something different, and fitted apart they give three answers.

rebuttals: One map and one clock first. Two clocks in one fit is the mistake that never shows up afterwards.
Fit all three together second. Fitted separately they give three answers and no way to choose.
Read the misses third, for pattern rather than size. A pattern is a force nobody modelled.
Carry it forward last. The burn happens later than the measurements, and the doubt grows on the way.
cards: Put every measurement on one map and one clock.
Fit one path to the distance, the angles and the pitch.
Look at what the fit misses, and why.
Carry the answer, and its range, to the burn.

title: What holds it in the curve
task: Say why the spacecraft needs speed to stay in that path.
scene: The return path swings the spacecraft round the Moon at two and a half thousand kilometres up. Somebody on the loop has asked why it does not simply fall onto the surface.
question: Why does the spacecraft need any speed at all to stay in that path?
takeaway: An orbit is falling, with enough sideways speed that the ground keeps curving away.
why: It is falling. It has been falling the whole way round. What stops it arriving is sideways speed: while gravity pulls it down, it moves along, and the Moon's surface curves away underneath at about the same rate. Too slow and the path meets the ground.
answerText: It is falling the whole way round. Its sideways speed means the surface curves away as fast as it drops.

choices: Its sideways speed turns constant falling into a curve around the Moon.
An outward force balances gravity, so nothing is pulling it anywhere.
Its speed weakens the Moon's pull on it.
Its forward motion holds it up, like a wing.
rebuttals: There is no outward force. The spacecraft is being pulled inward the whole time, which is what bends the path.
Speed does not weaken gravity. It changes the shape of the path that gravity produces.
There is no air out there to push against, and the engine is off for nearly all of it.

title: How a spacecraft turns
task: Match each change to what it does to the turning.
scene: The guidance computer is out and the crew is about to fly by hand. Before anybody touches a thruster, the room says plainly what each change does.
takeaway: Turning follows the same rules as moving. It is just harder to see them.
why: Four rules cover every hand-flown turn. The same push further from the middle turns harder, which is the one the crew can actually choose. The same push on a heavier, more spread-out craft turns it more slowly, and stops it more slowly too.

choices: It turns harder.
It turns more slowly.
The turning cancels out, and it ends up as it started.
The total turning cannot change, however things move inside.
rebuttals: The same push further out has more leverage, and it is the term the crew can actually choose.
The same push on something harder to turn gives less turning. Harder to start, and just as hard to stop.
Equal pushes for equal times cancel out. That is exactly what a start pulse and a stop pulse are.
Moving mass inside shifts the turning about between parts, and it cannot change the total.
scenarios: The same push, further from the middle.
The same push, on a craft that is harder to turn.
An equal push one way, then the other, for equal times.
Moving things about inside, with nothing pushing from outside.

title: Turning it by hand
task: Choose the opening pulse and where to start braking, then run the turn.
scene: The guidance computer is off. The crew has to turn the spacecraft ninety degrees using two thruster pairs and a mark on the window. Every extra correction spends fuel meant for the return.
question: How hard do you start the turn, and where do you start braking so it arrives still?
takeaway: Stopping the push does not stop the motion, so the braking has to start early.
why: A thruster pulse does not make a turn that stops itself. It changes how fast the spacecraft is turning, and when the pulse ends it keeps going at that rate. Stopping needs the opposite thruster, and that takes just as long as starting did.
answerText: Brake before the target. A six-second pulse gets it turning at twelve degrees a second, which takes about thirty-six degrees to stop, so braking starts near fifty-four.

fly.hint: Pick a start-pulse duration, then set the angle where the opposite thruster begins firing. The run ends only when the vehicle has stopped rotating.

shape.hint: Pick a start-pulse duration, then set the angle where the opposite thruster begins firing. The run ends only when the vehicle has stopped rotating.

title: Which push turns the ship?
task: Drag each thruster move to the motion it causes.
scene: Kwame Mensah, the dynamics lead, gives you four thruster buttons. They all use the same strength. Your job is to turn the spacecraft without wasting fuel.
takeaway: The same push can turn a spacecraft more or less depending on where it acts and which way it points.
why: A sideways push far from the middle makes a stronger turn than the same push near the middle. A push aimed through the middle mostly moves the craft instead of twisting it. To stop a turn, push the other way.
answerText: Use the far-out sideways thruster to start the turn, and the opposite thruster to stop it.

text.setup: Match each thruster move to what the spacecraft will do.
choices: Strong turn
Small turn
Mostly slides instead of turning
Slows or stops the turn
rebuttals: Farther from the middle gives the push more turning power.
The same push close to the middle still turns the ship, but less.
A push aimed through the middle does not have much twist.
An opposite twist takes rotation away.
scenarios: Fire a sideways thruster far from the middle.
Fire the same sideways thruster close to the middle.
Fire a thruster aimed straight through the middle.
While the ship is turning, fire the opposite turning thruster.

title: How long can the battery last?
task: Turn the store and the draw into hours.
scene: The fuel cells are gone, and the crew is on the entry batteries days earlier than any plan allowed. The flight doctor, who watches the crew's health from the ground, wants a number of hours before the next decision about switching things off.
question: How long will the batteries last?
takeaway: An amount divided by a rate is a time, and that time is what every other decision gets argued against.
why: There is a store and there is a draw, and dividing one by the other gives hours. Eighteen kilowatt hours at three kilowatts is six hours. It is an ideal figure. It assumes the draw stays flat and that every last bit of the store is usable, and neither is quite true.
answerText: About six hours, if the draw stays flat. It is a rough number, and everything today gets argued against it.

estimate.prompt: The entry batteries hold about 18 kilowatt hours that can actually be used. The things that must stay on draw about 3 kilowatts.
estimate.question: How long will the batteries last?
estimate.relationship: Hours = what is in the store ÷ how fast it is being used.
estimate.explanation: The bus voltage says how the energy is delivered, and nothing about how much there is. The time to the next burn is a deadline rather than an ingredient.
labels: 18 kWh (what is usable in the batteries)

title: Why is the voltage sagging?
task: Say which fault fits the voltage, the current and the heat together.
scene: A main power line is sagging at twenty-four volts instead of twenty-eight, while the current drawn from it sits where it was planned to be. Engineers want to start pulling equipment off.
question: Which fault fits the voltage, the current and the heat?
takeaway: Voltage, current and heat are three views of one fault, and one view is not enough.
why: Three readings, one fault, and each says something different. Something extra drawing power would show up as more current than planned. The current is where it should be. A failed supply would show as less coming in, and what comes in is normal. What is left is something in the path resisting.
answerText: A bad connection in the path. It eats voltage on the way through and turns it into heat, which is why the joint is warm.

choices: A bad connection somewhere in the path.
Something extra drawing power that nobody knows about.
The supply itself has failed.
Only the voltmeter is wrong.
choiceMechanisms: A resisting joint drops the voltage past it, and turns what it drops into heat.
An unexpected device pulls extra current and drags the bus down.
Less is coming in, so the battery has to make up the difference.
The bus is fine, and only one instrument is telling a story.
rebuttals: Something extra drawing power would show as more current than planned, and the current is where it should be.
A failed supply would show as less coming in. What is coming in is normal, so the fault is further along.
A bad voltmeter explains the reading and not the hot joint or the extra battery current. Two instruments agree.
text.headline: A main power line sags under a load that is exactly what was planned.

title: Switch things off without losing the mission
task: Share out the amp-hours, and keep every needed condition met.
scene: Forty-one amp-hours left, and sixty-two hours to fly. An amp-hour is one hour of giving one amp, so forty-one of them is not much. Guidance, radio, heating and life support all want power. Something has to be turned down within minutes.
question: How many hours of each can the spacecraft afford?
takeaway: A power budget is not a ranking of what matters. It is hours multiplied by draw, and the total is fixed.
why: This is not a list of what matters most. It is a sum. Every load costs its draw multiplied by the hours it runs, and the total cannot pass forty-one. Life support runs the whole way, so it is bought first. Guidance is needed in fixed windows, so those get booked.
answerText: Buy life support for the whole return. Book the guidance windows. Keep enough heating to protect the batteries. What is left pays for short radio windows.

allocate.hint: Set runtime for each load. The amp-hour total updates as current times hours, and the mission-condition panel shows what your allocation can still accomplish.

shape.hint: Set runtime for each load. The amp-hour total updates as current times hours, and the mission-condition panel shows what your allocation can still accomplish.

title: How much does the cabin cool?
task: Work out how far the temperature falls in three hours.
scene: With most things switched off, the cabin is losing about a kilowatt more heat than it makes. The flight doctor wants to know how long the crew has before the cold becomes a medical problem.
question: How far does the cabin cool over three hours?
takeaway: Big things change temperature slowly, and that slowness is time to think.
why: A kilowatt is a thousand joules leaking away every second. Three hours is about eleven thousand seconds, so the cabin loses roughly 11 million joules. That sounds enormous.
answerText: Under one degree. The cabin is heavy, so a kilowatt leaking for three hours barely moves it.

estimate.prompt: Over three hours the cabin loses about 11 million joules more than it makes. Warming this cabin by one degree takes about 12 million joules.
estimate.question: How far does the cabin cool over three hours?
estimate.relationship: Degrees lost = energy lost ÷ energy needed for one degree.
estimate.explanation: Both numbers are energies, so they divide straight into a number of degrees. The 4 °C is where the cabin is now, not how far it moves, and the three hours are already inside the eleven million.
estimate.solution: Eleven million shared out at twelve million for each degree is a bit under one degree.
labels: 12 million joules (to warm it one degree)

equations.e: degrees lost = energy lost ÷ energy for one degree

title: How the heat is getting out
task: Match each thing happening in the cabin to how the heat is moving.
scene: The cabin is cooling and the crew wants to do something about it. What they can do depends on how the heat is actually leaving, so the room names the route first.
takeaway: Naming the route is what tells you which fix would work at all.
why: Heat leaves three ways, and each has a different fix. By touching, which needs contact and is short range. By riding on moving air, which is why circulation spreads warmth about. And by beaming straight across a gap, which needs nothing in between and works fine in vacuum.

choices: Heat moving by touching.
Heat riding on moving air.
Heat beaming across a gap.
Heat conducted straight out along metal.
rebuttals: People in contact pass heat by touching. It is short range and it needs contact.
Air carrying warmth about the cabin is heat riding on something moving, rather than passing through it.
A cold wall soaking up warmth from across the cabin is heat beaming across a gap. It needs nothing in between.
A metal strut to the outside conducts all the way out, and it never stops. That is the leak that runs all night.
scenarios: Moving air carries warmth round the cabin.
A cold wall soaks up warmth from everything facing it.
A metal strut runs out to the structure outside.
columns: What is happening in the cabin

title: Keep the cabin survivable
task: Make the call before the next mission clock update.
scene: The cabin is at four degrees and falling. Water is beading on the walls and the crew is sleeping in their suits. Heating all of it is not affordable on what is left.
question: Four degrees and falling, on a fixed amount of energy. What do you spend it on?
takeaway: Slowing a loss keeps paying. Replacing it has to be paid again every time.
why: There are two ways to fight cold and they cost differently. Replacing heat means paying again the moment you stop. Slowing the loss keeps working after the spending stops, which is what matters when the energy is fixed.
answerText: Wrap the crew area and the batteries. Slowing the loss keeps paying after the energy is gone; reheating has to be paid for again every time.

choices: Wrap the crew area and the batteries, to slow the loss.
Spend the rest on short bursts of heating the whole cabin.
Run the fans all the time, so everywhere is the same temperature.
Heat the electronics bay, and let the crew rely on their suits.
rebuttals: Reheating the whole cabin replaces what has gone and does nothing about the next hour. The same energy gets spent again.
Running the fans evens the temperature out and costs power the whole time, and it does not slow anything leaving.
Protecting the electronics keeps the hardware and lets the crew and the batteries go on cooling.

title: Follow the air
task: Build the air path in order, then name the link that is holding it up.
scene: Carbon dioxide keeps climbing. The scrubber, which is the machine that takes that gas back out of the air, has a fan that sounds normal and draws its usual current. The airflow through it is low. There are pressure readings on both sides of the filter.
question: Where does the air path become the problem?
takeaway: A chain moves at the rate of its most restricted link, not the rate of its noisiest one.
why: The fan makes a push. How much air moves depends on everything downstream of it. Normal current only proves the fan has power. The pressure difference across the filter is large and the flow is small, which is what a blockage looks like.
answerText: The filter. The fan is fine, and almost nothing is getting past that filter, so nothing reaches the scrubber.

text.headline: Cabin carbon dioxide rises even though the scrubber fan still draws power.

chain.hint: Put the air-transfer links in physical order. Then use the observed flow and pressure pattern to name the one required link that governs the entire loop.

links.label: Scrubber fan
links.transfers: pressure rise to the moving air

links.label: Filter section
links.reading: large pressure drop across this section

links.label: CO2 sorbent bed
links.transfers: carbon dioxide from air into sorbent

links.label: Return duct
links.transfers: treated air back to the cabin

equations.about: how much of a store gets used

shape.hint: Put the air-transfer links in physical order. Then use the observed flow and pressure pattern to name the one required link that governs the entire loop.

title: How much they breathe out
task: Work out how much carbon dioxide the crew makes in six hours.
scene: Three crew, each breathing out about twenty litres of carbon dioxide an hour. The workshop needs to know what a home-made scrubber has to keep up with over the next six hours.
question: How much carbon dioxide do they make in six hours?
takeaway: The rate something arrives at sets the smallest rate that can remove it.
why: Three people at twenty litres an hour make sixty litres an hour between them. Six hours of that is three hundred and sixty. That number is the bar. Anything that removes carbon dioxide more slowly than the crew makes it does not hold the level steady. It only makes the rise slower.
answerText: About 360 litres. Sixty litres an hour between the three of them, for six hours.

estimate.prompt: Three crew each breathe out about twenty litres of carbon dioxide an hour, and the scrubber has to keep up for six hours.
estimate.question: How much carbon dioxide do they make in six hours?
estimate.relationship: Total = what one person makes an hour × how many people × how many hours.
estimate.explanation: A rate for one person needs a head count and a stretch of time, and both have to match the question. The daily figure describes the same crew and cannot be used here without more work.

title: Make the air breathable
task: Make the call before the next mission clock update.
scene: Carbon dioxide is close to the limit and still climbing. The spare canisters are square, the socket is round, and there is tape, a suit hose, a sock and a plastic cover.
question: Tape, a hose, a sock and a plastic cover. What does the fix have to get right?
takeaway: Nothing gets cleaned unless it goes through the thing that cleans it.
why: Two things have to be true, and only one of them is obvious. There has to be something that takes the carbon dioxide out, and every bit of air has to be made to go through it. Air is lazy.
answerText: A sealed path, so the air has nowhere to go but through. A gap round the canister undoes everything else.

choices: A sealed path, so the air has to go through the canister.
As much of the canister exposed to the cabin as possible.
Readings taken in several places round the cabin.
A fan loud enough that the crew can hear it running.
rebuttals: Exposing more of it only helps the air that reaches it. A big canister with a gap round it cleans less than a small one taped tight.
Measuring in several places is how they find out whether it worked. That is necessary and it is not the fix.
A fan they can hear proves a motor is turning. It says nothing about how much air is moving, or where it goes.

title: Why did the signal fade?
task: Change one thing at a time, and put it back, until the fade follows something.
scene: Voice and data have gone weak at two ground stations at once. A ground station is a dish antenna on Earth, and these two are on opposite sides of the world. The spacecraft's transmitter is putting out what it should. Three things can be swapped without risking anything.
question: Which change makes the fade appear and disappear?
takeaway: A cause is proved when the effect follows the change both ways.
why: Several things can weaken a radio link, and only one test settles which. Swap to a different ground receiver and nothing changes, so it is not one receiver. Swap the transmitter chain and nothing changes, so it is not the transmitter.
answerText: Where the antenna is pointing. Correcting it brings the signal back, and putting the error back makes it fade again. Neither swap changes anything.

text.headline: Voice and telemetry suddenly become weak.

control.hint: Run one reversible test at a time. A cause has to produce a response larger than the noise and reproduce that response when the change is reversed.

shape.hint: Run one reversible test at a time. A cause has to produce a response larger than the noise and reproduce that response when the change is reversed.

title: Build a stronger radio link
task: Match each change to what it does to the signal.
scene: Naomi Ito, the communications lead, has a weak radio link to the spacecraft. You can change one thing at a time before the next navigation update.
question: Which changes help the signal reach the ground clearly?
takeaway: A radio link works better when the antennas point at each other, the path is clear, and the receiver can separate the signal from noise.
why: A radio signal can be perfectly real and still be hard to hear. Pointing matters. Distance matters. Noise matters. Changing one thing at a time lets the team learn what is actually hurting the link instead of guessing.
answerText: Point the dish more accurately, reduce nearby interference, and use the station with the clearer path. Turning away from the spacecraft makes the link worse.

choices: Point the dish more accurately
Re-acquire the spacecraft and lock back on
Reduce nearby radio noise
Use the ground station with the clearer path
rebuttals: Better pointing puts more of the signal into the receiver.
Turning away throws away signal instead of recovering it.
Less nearby noise makes a weak signal easier to separate.
A clearer path gives the receiver a better chance to hear the spacecraft.

scenarios.label: Dish is a little off target
Local equipment is making radio noise
One station has a clearer view

title: Get the link back
task: Put the four moves in order.
scene: The signal is weak and drifting. The crew is answering calls it can barely hear. The next navigation update depends on getting the link back.
takeaway: Do the biggest and cheapest thing first, and let each move buy the next.
why: Pointing is the biggest thing on the list and the cheapest to fix, so it goes first. Slowing the message down comes next. Less is being sent, so less signal is needed to read it, and nothing aboard has to change.

rebuttals: Pointing first. It is the biggest term in the sum, and the cheapest one to fix.
Slowing the message down second. A slower message needs less signal, and it costs nothing aboard.
The big dishes third, told where to listen, because the signal has drifted in frequency.
Navigation last. Getting the link back also produces the measurements the burn needs.
cards: Check where the spacecraft is pointing.
Slow the message down, and listen over a narrower range.
Point the big ground dishes, and tell them where to listen.
Feed the tracking that comes back into the navigation.

title: What is shaking it?
task: Say which explanation fits how the shaking depends on speed.
scene: A bad vibration only appears when the wheel runs near one speed. Above and below that it dies away. Two sensors on different parts of the structure see the same narrow band.
question: Which explanation fits the readings?
takeaway: What matters is not how hard it shakes, but what is shaking it, and how fast.
why: Everything has a rhythm it likes to shake at, the way a swing does. Push a swing at any old moment and little happens. Push it in time with itself and it goes higher every push.
answerText: The wheel is pushing in time with the structure's own rhythm. That is why it only happens in a narrow band of speed.

choices: The wheel is pushing in time with the structure's own rhythm.
One sensor has come loose and is rattling.
Something hit it once, and this is the after-effect.
The structure is breaking up.
choiceMechanisms: A repeated push lands in time with the structure's rhythm, and the shaking builds.
One sensor rattles on its own mount while the structure is quiet.
A single knock rings the structure, whatever the wheel is doing.
Damage shakes everything, at all speeds and all frequencies.
rebuttals: A loose sensor rattles on its own mount. A second sensor somewhere else sees exactly the same thing.
A single knock does not care what speed the wheel is running at, and nothing recorded an impact.
Breaking up shakes at every speed. This is narrow, repeatable, and it stops when the speed changes.
text.headline: A bad vibration appears only in a narrow band of wheel speed.

title: How far to stay clear
task: Work out the highest speed that is safely below the bad band.
scene: The bad band runs from three thousand one hundred to three thousand three hundred turns a minute. The rule is to stay two hundred clear of it, and the pump still has to run.
question: What is the highest speed that is safely below the band?
takeaway: Avoiding a resonance is arithmetic on the band, not a matter of running gently.
why: A resonance is a band rather than a point, and a margin either side of it is what stops the pump wandering back in. The band starts at three thousand one hundred.
answerText: Two thousand nine hundred turns a minute. The band starts at 3,100, and the rule is 200 clear of it.

estimate.prompt: The bad band runs from 3,100 to 3,300 turns a minute. The rule is to stay 200 clear of it.
estimate.question: What is the highest speed that is safely below the band?
estimate.relationship: Highest safe speed = the bottom of the band − the clearance.
estimate.explanation: Work off the bottom of the band, not the worst point in the middle of it. Using 3,200 puts the pump inside the band it is meant to avoid.

title: Stop the shaking
task: Say which change stops the pushes landing in time.
scene: A panel shakes whenever the pump runs near one speed, and it has grown worse over three cycles. The pump is needed, and its speed can still be changed from the panel.
question: Which change stops the pushes landing in time with the panel?
takeaway: Change what is pushing, when you cannot change what is being pushed.
why: This kind of shaking needs two things: a structure with a rhythm, and something pushing in time with it. In flight, changing what is pushing is far easier than changing the structure.
answerText: Move the pump speed off the band. It stops the pushes landing in time, and it can be undone at once.

choices: Move the pump's speed away from the band.
Deaden the panel, so the shaking dies away.
Measure it in a few more places first.
Run the pump harder, to get through the band quickly.
rebuttals: Deadening it bleeds the energy away and is the right permanent fix. It needs hardware, access and somebody's hands on the structure.
Measuring in more places is how you check the fix worked. It is the check rather than the fix.
Getting through quickly assumes the structure survives the crossing, which is exactly what three growing cycles have called into question.

title: Really off course, or one bad clock?
task: Say which explanation fits all four measurements.
scene: Two ground measurements suddenly put the spacecraft ahead of where it should be. They agree with each other. A star camera and the spacecraft's own sensors are on the board too.
question: Which measurements moved on their own, and which moved together?
takeaway: When measurements agree, ask whether they agree separately or share a part.
why: Agreement counts only when the things agreeing could have failed apart. Range and Doppler both use the same ground clock, so one late clock moves them together. The star camera does not use that clock, and it still matches the prediction.
answerText: One shared clock. The measurements that moved all use it, and the star camera, which does not, still agrees with the prediction.

choices: The spacecraft really is off course.
One shared clock is wrong, and it moved everything that uses it.
Several instruments failed separately, at the same time.
The star camera has failed.
choiceMechanisms: It has actually moved away from the predicted path.
One shared timestamp shifts everything worked out from it, together.
Unrelated instruments happen to drift the same way at the same moment.
The star camera alone is producing a wrong answer.
rebuttals: Moving off course needs a push, and the onboard readings show no push at all.
Separate failures do not drift the same way at the same moment. These share a clock.
A failed star camera would put its answer in the wrong place. It is the one that agrees with the prediction.

trace.decision: Decide whether the spacecraft really moved or several measurements share one late clock.

title: How much room is left
task: Work out how much clear space is left either side.
scene: The entry corridor is forty kilometres wide. The circle of doubt around the spacecraft's position is ten kilometres across. Sandoval needs a margin before the burn is called.
question: How much clear space is left on each side, if it flies down the middle?
takeaway: A route is planned against the doubt, not against the line drawn through the middle of it.
why: The corridor is forty kilometres wide, so aiming down the middle puts twenty either side. The spacecraft could be five kilometres off in any direction, so five of those twenty are already spent before anybody makes a mistake. Fifteen is what is left.
answerText: Fifteen kilometres each side. Twenty from the middle of the corridor, less five for how far off the spacecraft might be.

estimate.prompt: The corridor is 40 kilometres wide. The circle of doubt around the position is 10 kilometres across.
estimate.question: How much clear space is left on each side, if it flies down the middle?
estimate.explanation: Take the doubt off the corridor first, then split what is left between the two sides. Both are widths, so both belong to the whole corridor rather than to one edge of it.
estimate.solution: Forty take away ten is thirty. Down the middle, that is 15 kilometres on each side.

title: Say it before you do it
task: Predict what the burn will do, fire it, then measure it.
scene: The correction burn is ready. It adds 3 metres a second, 12 hours before the spacecraft reaches the air. Carter wants the prediction written down first.
question: Predict how far the burn moves the landing point, fire it, and then measure.
takeaway: A burn that happened is not a burn that worked. Only the measurement afterwards says so.
why: Three metres every second sounds like nothing. Keep it up for 12 hours and it is a long way. Three metres a second is about 11 kilometres an hour. Eleven, for 12 hours, is roughly 130 kilometres. Say that number out loud first.
answerText: About 130 kilometres — and only the tracking pass afterwards shows whether it really moved that far.

verify.hint: Write the prediction first. It cannot be changed afterwards, which is the whole point of writing it first.
verify.unmeasuredMoral: The engine fired and nobody looked. A burn that happened is not the same as a burn that worked.

title: Four minutes of silence
task: Make the call before the next mission clock update.
scene: For four minutes in the middle of entry there is no radio at all. The room knows it is coming, and Carter still wants somebody to say why it happens.
question: Why does the radio go quiet for four minutes?
takeaway: Some silences are physics rather than faults, and nothing on the ground can shorten one.
why: The capsule hits the air at enormous speed, and the air in front of it has nowhere to go. Being squeezed that hard makes it hot, hot enough to glow, and that glowing layer wraps the whole capsule. Radio waves cannot get through it.
answerText: The air around the capsule is squeezed until it glows, and glowing air will not let radio through.

choices: Glowing hot air wraps the capsule and blocks radio.
The antenna is switched off to save battery.
The capsule is behind the Moon at that point.
The radio is broken by the shaking of entry.
rebuttals: Nothing is switched off. The radio is transmitting the whole time and nothing gets out.
The Moon is far behind them by entry. They are at the Earth.
Nothing breaks. The radio works again by itself once the capsule slows down.

title: The order the silence forces
task: Put the entry steps in order around the four minutes of silence.
scene: Everything now depends on eleven minutes, and four of them have no radio at all. Anything that needs the ground has to happen before the silence starts.
takeaway: When part of a plan cannot be changed, everything that might need changing goes before it.
why: Four minutes of silence sets the whole order. Anything that needs a decision from the ground has to be settled first, because during the silence there is nobody to ask. Who is flying gets agreed before the silence, not during it.

rebuttals: Attitude and settings first, before entry. Nothing here can be changed through four minutes of silence.
Agree who is flying before committing. That is not something to work out while nobody can talk.
Watching the slowing comes third. It cannot start before entry, because there is nothing to compare yet.
Descent last, with the record kept. This is the only flight that will ever produce this data.
cards: Set the approved attitude and settings before the silence.
Agree who is flying, before the radio goes quiet.
Watch the slowing and the heating against what was predicted.
Come down, keeping the record of what happened.

title: What the review should fix
task: Say which proposal removes the cause rather than improving the response.
scene: The crew is aboard the recovery ship and the review board meets Monday. Four proposals compete for three funded places.
question: Which proposal deserves first place, because it removes the cause?
takeaway: Fixing what caused it outlasts getting better at coping with it.
why: The same weakness appeared twice on this flight. Three pressure readings shared one circuit, and later several tracking numbers shared one clock. Both times, agreement looked far stronger than it was, and both times somebody nearly acted on it. Removing those shared parts is the only proposal that stops it happening again.
answerText: Remove the shared parts. Everything else on the list helps people cope with the same failure rather than preventing it.

choices: Redesign the shared circuits and shared clocks, so agreement means something.
Keep the full records of telemetry, settings and decisions.
Improve the simulator, and rehearse failures more.
Put more people on the anomaly desk for future flights.
rebuttals: Keeping the records is how anybody reconstructs it afterwards, and it leaves the shared parts exactly where they are.
Rehearsing improves how people handle the same failure. It does not stop the shared clock failing again.
More people can diagnose it faster, and the shared part is still there to fail.
